did.unittitle: Miscellaneous Personal Papers Collection

descriptivenote.p: In English.

did.abstract: The Miscellaneous Personal Papers record group is an open collection consisting of the correspondence, diaries, writings and/or other papers and memorabilia of various individuals. This collection contains papers of individuals who were Yale faculty members, alumni/ae, clergy, ecumenical workers, or missionaries in areas other than China.

accessrestrict.head: Conditions Governing Access
accessrestrict.p: The materials are open for research.

bioghist.head: Biographical / Historical
bioghist.p: See the alphabetical listing for biographical information about the individuals included in this record group.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: This collection contains correspondence, diaries, writings and/or other papers and memorabilia of various individuals, including former Yale faculty members, clergymen and missionaries to areas other than China. The papers of these men and women have been placed in the Miscellaneous Personal Papers record group because the quantity or substance of the material did not warrant a separate record group.

prefercite.head: Preferred Citation
prefercite.p: Miscellaneous Personal Papers Collection (RG 30), Special Collections, Yale Divinity Library.

processinfo.head: Processing Information
processinfo.p: Place names were modernized in the description, with the name originally used in the collection material or in an older version of the finding aid in parenthesis: e.g. "Beijing (Peking)" or "Benin (Dahomey)".

Charlotte Hazen Atlee White Rowe

bioghist.head: Biographical / Historical
bioghist.p: Charlotte Hazen Atlee White Rowe (1782-1863) was born in Lancaster, PA. Orphaned at age eleven, she went to live in Rutland, MA where she later met and married merchant Nathaniel White. After the death of White and her son with him, Charlotte moved to Haverhill, MA and joined the Baptist Church there. Also living in this area were Ann Hasseltine who married Adoniram Judson and Harriet Atwood who married Samuel Newell, early Congregational missionaries. Charlotte later moved to Philadelphia where she joined the Samsom Street Baptist Church. At this time the Baptist were forming a national organization for international missions. Adoniram Judson, who had initially gone to the mission field as a Congregationalist was appointed as the first Baptist missionary but his wife Ann was considered a volunteer assistant missionary.

In 1814 Charlotte helped form and lead the Sansom Street Baptist Female Society for Promoting Evangelical Missions. In 1815 the Baptist mission board appointed George Hough and Charlotte White to join the Judson mission work in Burma, causing a controversy because Charlotte was a woman and not an ordained man. While at a stopover in Calcutta, Charlotte met and married Joshua Rowe, a British Baptist misisonary who was a widower with three young sons. Instead of proceeding to Burma, Charlotte served with Joshua in India under the auspices of the British Baptist Missionary Society. She learned Hindi and advocated for education for girls and women. Charlotte and Joshua had three children together, twin daughters and a son. When Joshua died, Charlotte was left as a single parent of six children. She self-funded her continuing missionary work overseeing several schools and worship sites for eleven years but eventually financial pressures forced her to return to Britain to seek official appointment by the British Baptists. After three years in England, Charlotte and her children returned to the U.S.

In 1910 he established his own missionary and educational work under the name of the Alpha and Omega Assembly, based in New Haven, CT and Brooklyn NY.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Many of the signatures in the album are of religious leaders of the northeastern United States. Notable among the signees is J.W.C. Pennington (1807-1870), author of The Fugitive Blacksmith , who attended Yale from 1834 to 1837 and was awarded a posthumous N.A. Privatim degree by Yale in April, 2023. Pennington was ordained as a minister in the Congregational Church, later also serving Presbyterian churches in Hartford, Connecticut and New York. Pennington's signature is dated June 28, 1857.

did.unittitle: Beardslee, Alvord

bioghist.head: Biographical / Historical
bioghist.p: Beardslee received a B.D. from Yale Divinity School in 1953 and an S.T.M. in 1955. He served as a Professor of Religion at Hollins College, VA and as Congregational minister in the United Church of Christ, Salisbury. He was a Research Fellow at YDS in 1981-1982 and 1989-1990. He served on the Alumnal Board of YDS and was a Trustee of the Foundation for the Preservation of Sterling Divinity Quadrangle. These personal papers of Beardslee complement documentation regarding YDS and the Save the Quad movement in Record Group No. 53, YDS Memorabilia.

Beecher, William H.

bioghist.head: Biographical / Historical
bioghist.p: This may be William Henry Beecher (1802-1899), son of the Reverend Lyman Beecher and Roxana Foote Beecher of Litchfield, Connecticut. As a young man he apprenticed as a cabinetmaker in Hartford and New Milford, Connecticut, as well as New York, New York. William later attended Andover Theological Seminary and received an honorary Masters degree from Yale College. In 1830 he became a licensed preacher. His first position as minister was in Newport, Rhode Island. William then worked at various churched in Middletown, Connecticut; Putnam, Ohio; Batavia, New York; Euclid, Ohio; and North Brookfield, Massachusetts.

did.unittitle: Bilheimer, Robert

bioghist.head: Biographical / Historical
bioghist.p: Bilheimer graduated from Yale Divinity School in 1945. He helped to organize the first meeting of the World Council of Churches in 1948 and served as a WCC associate general secretary. From 1963 he was senior minister of Central Presbyterian Church in Rochester, NY, returning to ecumenical work in 1966 as director of the international affairs program of the National Council of Churches. He was executive director of the Institute for Ecumenical and Cultural Research in Collegeville, MN before retiring in 1984.

Bowler, Henry Reginald

bioghist.head: Biographical / Historical
bioghist.p: Bowler served as Secretary of the Laymen's Foreign Mission Inquiry Commission of Appraisal during its nine month journey around the world in 1931-1932. The Commission of Appraisal, led by Harvard professor William Ernest Hocking, studied the foreign mission work of six mainline Protestant denominations in India, Burma, China, and Japan. Bowler managed the Commission's travel arrangements and secretarial work.

Bowler (1889-1976) was born in Milford, Nebraska. He graduated from Linfield College in McMinnville, Oregon and received a Rhodes Scholarship to study English at Oxford from 1913 to 1916. When he returned to the United States he worked for the YMCA War Services Division in New York City and as a secretary to John R. Mott. From 1921 until 1958 he worked for the Northern Baptist Convention in New York City in a variety of positions.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: The collection includes 37 typewritten letters from Bowler to his wife that provide detailed description of the his activities with the Commission. See additional records related to the Laymen's Foreign Mission Inquiry Commission in the Yale Divinity Library' HR1276 holdings.

Burhans, Daniel

bioghist.head: Biographical / Historical
bioghist.p: Daniel Burhans (1763-1853) was a cleric in the Anglican and later Episcopal Church in New England. Burhans was educated as a layreader under Gideon Bostwick (1742-1793) in Lanesborough, Massachusetts. Upon Bostwick's death, Burhans was ordained to the priesthood and became the rector of the churches in Lanesborough, Great Barrington, and Lenox. In 1798, he became rector of Trinity Episcopal Church in Newtown, Connecticut.

did.unittitle: Bound collection of sermons

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: This collection contains both sermons written by Daniel Burhans and sermons gathered by him written by prominent Anglican and later Episcopal clergy throughout the Northeast. Notable within the volume is a sermon most likely by Agur Treadwell (1734-1763, Yale 1760) on the Seven Years' War (French and Indian War) and a sermon by John Rutger Marshall (1743-1793) on the attitudes and expectations in the American colonies in the months before the Declaration of Independence. Further sermons are from Burhans' predecessors at Trinity Church in Newtown, Connecticut John Beach (1700-1782, Yale 1721) and Philo Perry (1752-1798, Yale 1777), his mentor the Massachusetts cleric Gideon Bostwick (1742-1793, Yale 1762), and David Botsford (1797-1822, Yale 1818).

Clarke, Walter and Samuel

bioghist.head: Biographical / Historical
bioghist.p: Walter Clarke (1812-1871) was born in Middletown, Connecticut, the son of Warner and Abigail Clarke. He graduated from Yale College in 1837. Following a few years teaching at the Waterbury Academy and the College of Mobile (Alabama), he began his studies at the Yale Divinity School, graduating in 1840. Clarke was ordained as pastor of the First Congregational Church in Canterbury, Connecticut in 1842 and then served the South Church in Hartford from 1845 to 1859. It was during this time in Hartford that Clarke was involved in the theological controversy that pitted conservative church leaders against acclaimed minister of Hartford's North Church, Horace Bushnell. Clarke was a member of the five-person committee that was appointed in June 1849 to study Bushnell's works. The committee presented three reports after a 3-2 vote in favor of Bushnell' s exoneration. The first report addressed procedural matters and was approved unanimously. The majority report, representing the three Bushnell supporters, demonstrated that the Hartford minister ought to be exonerated of all charges of heresy. The detailed minority report was presented by Clarke and Joel Hawes. Clarke served the Mercer Street Presbyterian Church in New York City from 1859 to 1861 and then was pastor at the First Presbyterian Church in Buffalo, NY for the last ten years of his life. Walter Clarke married Mary A. Clark in 1839. Following her death in 1849 he married Elizabeth Grew.

Samuel Taylor Clarke was born in 1843, the son of Walter and Mary Clarke. He graduated from Hamilton College in 1862 and studied theology at Union Theological Seminary in New York City. Samuel became pastor of a church in Detroit, Michigan and later of Presbyterian churches in Oswego and Elmira, New York. He married Fanny Stephens in 1868 and they had a daughter, Edith, in 1871.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Papers of Walter Clarke and his son Samuel T. Clarke provide an interesting glimpse into clergy life in the second half of the 19th century. Notable in this collection are letters exchanged between Walter Clarke and Horace Bushnell, who was minister at Hartford's North Church while Clarke was minister at Hartford's South Church. Clarke was among the conservative churchmen who unsuccessfully sought to expel Bushnell as a heretic. Bushnell's church unanimously withdrew from the local consociation in 1852, thus removing any possibility of further action against him. Clarke's letters to and from Bushnell from the years 1854-1858 refer to Clarke's role on the committee that prepared reports for the ruling on Bushnell's status.

The collection also contains correspondence and documents of Walter Clarke's son Samuel T. Clarke, who was also a minister. A very complete collection of receipts from the years 1870 to 1893 provide detailed information about Samuel's purchures and his involvement as a landlord for properties in the area of Elmira, New York.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Two detailed letters from Clarke to Bushnell date from March and May, 1854. Three letters from Bushnell to Clarke date from 1856, 1858 and undated. The letters relate to the theological controversy that pitted conservative church leaders against Horace Bushnell when he was minister of North Church in Hartford 1849-1854. See also Horace Bushnell papers in Record Group 39.

did.unittitle: Walter Clarke to / from Noah Porter

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: One letter from Clarke to Porter and Porter's reply relate to the theological controversy surrounding Horace Bushnell, minister at North Church in Hartford. Noah Porter of Farmington was a member, along with Walter Clarke, of the five-person committee appointed by the Hartford Central Association to make a recommendation regarding Bushnell. Clarke and Joel Hawes were the minority on the committee who recommended Bushnell's removal but the majority, including Porter, recommended against expulsion.

bioghist.head: Biographical / Historical
bioghist.p: John Crump was born in New London, Connecticut in 1814. Following his graduation from Yale College he studied Medicine and went to the South due to ill health but he returned to New London and died of pulmonary consumption on July 4, 1835.

did.unittitle: Manuscript journal kept by a Yale College student

acqinfo.head: Immediate Source of Acquisition
acqinfo.p: Gift of Kenneth Minkema in honor of Yale Divinity School's bicentennial in 2022.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Crump began his spiritual autobiography at the suggestion of Prof. Nathaniel William Taylor, Dwight Professor of Didactic Theology at Yale and chief architect of the revisionist "New Haven School" of theology. Throughout, Crump mentions Taylor and other professors and administrators in the College, who are encouraging a general revival of religion going on in the town and among the students. He also refers to a number of fellow students, alums, and friends, all of whom are caught up in the prayer meetings, public worship services, private gatherings in the dormitory, and personal conversations around the questions of devotion, conversion, and duty. Over all, the diary gives us a brief but valuable glimpse into a time of intense religious fervor, dubbed by scholars as the Second Great Awakening, not only in New Haven but throughout Connecticut. This note and a typed transcript of the journal have been provided by its donor, Kenneth Minkema, Executive Editor of The Works of Jonathan Edwards and Director of the Jonathan Edwards Center at YDS.

Day, George Edward

bioghist.head: Biographical / Historical
bioghist.p: George Edward Day was born in 1815, son of Gad Day and Roxanna Rice Day. He graduated from Yale College in 1833 and then taught two years in the Institution for the Deaf and Dumb in New York City. He graduated from Yale Divinity School in 1838 and was Instructor in Sacred Literature in the Yale Divinity School for two years before entering the ministry, serving churches in Marlboro and Northhampton, MA. Following ten years in the ministry Day served for 15 years as Professor of Biblical Literature in the Lane Theological Seminary at Cincinnati, OH. In 1866 he returned to YDS as Professor of the Hebrew Language and Literature and Biblical Theology. In 1888 he became Dean of the Divinity School, and for three or four years thereafter shared the duties of his professorship with Professor William Rainey Harper. Upon Day's retirement from the Office of Dean in 1895, he was made Professor Emeritus. Day and his wife Olivia Hotchkiss Day were the benefactors of the Day Missions Library at YDS, established in 1891. Day died in 1905.

Dirks, J. Edward

bioghist.head: Biographical / Historical
bioghist.p: 1940 - B.A., Dubuque; 1943 - B.D., YDS; 1947 - Ph.D., Columbia; 1955-1958 - Associate Professor Religion in Higher Education, Yale Divinity School; 1958-1967 - Stephen Merrell Clement Professor of Christian Methods, YDS; 1967-1968 - Research Consultant, YDS.

did.unittitle: Addresses, Lectures, and Papers: Writings related to religion in higher education. Sample titles: "The Religious Dimension in Education", "The Community of Faith and the Community of Learning", and "A Theology of the Campus Christian Ministry" given at the Danforth Conference for Campus Christian Workers. Dirks' licensure and ordination lecture, "Justification by Faith", is included.

Yale Divinity School: Danforth Program: The Danforth Study of Campus Ministries, sponsored by the Danforth Foundation beginning in 1963, was directed by Kenneth Underwood, a YDS colleague of Dirks. The project documented the state of religious awareness and commitment on American university and college campuses.

Travel Diary: Documents Dirks' travels from February through June of 1957, in India, Asia, and the Middle East. Entries are primarily reflections on the various discussions Dirks had with professors, students, administrators, and church leaders concerning universities and higher education in general within these countries.

Shorter Publications: A variety of different theological publications containing articles written by and about Dirks. Sample titles: "Commemoration Day Address: 1964" and "The Pursuit of Learning to the Glory of God" in the Wesleyan Studies in Religion .
Sermons written by Dirks. Many of these sermons appear to be given within academic setting. Several were given at Yale Divinity School
One letter between the Office of the Dean at Yale Divinity School and Dirks

Longer Publications: Introductions, chapters, and drafts of books written by Dirks. Sample titles: "The Contemporary University World: Freedom and Responsibility in the Higher Learning of Today", "Impressions of Christian Colleges in Asia", and "The Christian Community at Study: (chapter I) A Theology of Knowledge for the Christian Educational Community".

Durand, Charles S.

bioghist.head: Biographical / Historical
bioghist.p: Dr. C.S. Durand (1859-1931) served as a medical missionary with the Foreign Christian Missionary Society (Disciples of Christ) in India beginning in 1889. In Harda, Durand founded a hospital and worked closely with people affected with leprosy. His wife, Emma Minter Durand, worked in religious education for local women and girls. At an unknown date, C.S. Durand moved to Mussoorie, India. Emma and their daughter Mabel (alternatively spelled Mabelle) moved to Colorado Springs, Colorado around 1895. The letters at Yale Divinity Special Collections date from 1895-1907 during Durand's time in India and are mostly addresssed to Mabel in Colorado Springs. Other materials, including a small set of photographs from Rome following WWII, come from relatives of Mabel.

Elliott, Arthur James

bioghist.head: Biographical / Historical
bioghist.p: "Dad" A.J.Elliott (1875-1952) served the YMCA Student Division from 1907 to 1951. During the last sixteen years he was executive secretary of Christian evangelism among youth and led the student conferences held at Lake Geneva. Elliott traveled to Japan, China, and the Philippines in 1925 on behalf of the Student YMCA. In 1935 he was sent on a similar mission around the world. For additional biographical information see pamphlet Touchdowns for the Lord in the library's cataloged collection. See additional A.J. Elliott correspondence in Record Group No. 58, YMCA Student Division Archives.

bioghist.head: Biographical / Historical
bioghist.p: Mehitable Evarts (1774-1851) was the daughter of Roger Sherman, signer of the U.S. Declaration of Independence. After the death of her first husband, Daniel Barnes, she married Jeremiah Evarts, Christian activist and defender of Native American rights. The Evarts were based in the Boston area, though Jeremiah traveled frequently; he died in Charlston, South Carolina in 1831. Mehitable's sister Elizabeth Baldwin lived in New Haven.

did.unittitle: 22 letters from Mehitable Evarts to her sister Elizabeth Baldwin

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: These substantive letters deal mostly with family matters, including the health status, travels, and daily activities. The travels of Mehitable's husband Jeremiah Evarts are mentioned but there is little information about his activities. The letters refer to individuals and events in New Haven, where her sister Elizabeth lived.

did.unittitle: A series of newsletters prepared by Hill from 1960 to 1988. These newsletters were distributed in the churches served by Hill and/or sent by mail to a network of individuals who shared his concerns. Newsletters in this collection include: "Interpretation" 1960 Apr - 1961 Apr (18 issues); "The Contender" 1960 Sep - 1965 Mar, 1969 Jan (14 issues); "Church and World" 1964 Oct - 1984 Jun (146 issues); "The Hill Newsletter" 1984 Sep - 1988 Feb (43 issues); "The Hill Newsletter", which was issued jointly by Hill and his wife, Elizabeth Keeney Hill, has been compiled and indexed in a looseleaf notebook. The following description of "The Hill Newsletter" is taken from the introduction to the compilation: "(The Hill Newsletter) was distributed nationally and served as a major networking mechanism for peace advocates. It was also devoted to social issues, politics, national and international affairs, culture, religion, spirituality, and church integrity. It represents a candid, honest effort to transcend institutionalism and hypocrisy in American life, and to apply the principles of Jesus directly to current affairs. As such, it represents a unique commentary on American religious, political, and social life over the period from 1957 to 1988." Donors: Elizabeth K. Hill, James W. Hill.

Hovey, Gail

bioghist.head: Biographical / Historical
bioghist.p: Hovey was among the founders of the "Zambia Group," a small community of persons with a common history in the National Student Christian Federation/University Christian Movement who first met in Zambia in 1967. Most of the participants were involved in the Frontier Internship in Mission program and other programs initiated by Margaret Flory. The "Zambia Group" remained a community for some thirty years, centered on with a focus on concern for southern Africa. At annual meetings they focused on strategies for change in southern Africa and their relationships to those strategies. They sought one another's counsel about vocational, relational and resource decisions, pooling money to support activities both in the U.S. and in Africa for the liberation of southern Africa.

did.unittitle: Zambia Group files

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: The Zambia Group files include minutes of annual meetings and financial records, including letters of acknowledgement from organizations supported by the group, such as the American Committee on Africa and SWAPO. There is extensive correspondence between members, both quarterly group letters and individual letters to the keeper of these files, Gail (Morlan) Hovey. See the first folder for additional information about the group. Documentation of the activities of group members complements other collections at Yale Divinity Special Collections, including the Washington Office on Africa archives and Episcopal Churchpeople for Southern Africa archives. There are also strong links to Frontier Internship in Mission records; most members of the Zambia Group were Frontier Interns. The files also provide an interesting snapshot of life issues for a group of educated liberal Christian activists and educators in the second half of the 20th century.

Huntington, Lynde

bioghist.head: Biographical / Historical
bioghist.p: Lynde Huntington (1767–1804) was born in Lebanon, Connecticut. By the end of his sophomore year at Yale College, Huntington professed his faith and united with the College Church. He graduated in 1788 and spent several years out of school before returning to study theology. Lynde Huntington was licensed by the Windham Association in May, 1793, after which he spent time visiting congregations across Connecticut, until he was offered a permanent position as minister of the First Congregational Church and Society of Branford in the summer of 1795. It was there he met the widow of his predecessor, Anne Williams, whom he married in 1796. Huntington spent the remainder of his life ministering in this role up until 1804, when he died of consumption (Tuberculosis) at the age of 38.

did.unittitle: Spiritual Diary

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: The spiritual diary of Lynde Huntington is made up of Huntington's personal reflections on his practices of Calvinist orthodoxy and the state of his soul, along with remarks on books he read and sermons he heard. In the diary, Huntington expresses many feelings of frustration, anxiety, and depression.

did.unittitle: Original copies of "What Then Are We To Do?" sheets (1953 Sep 20 - 1971 May 30, 1978 Jun 18). (1 of 2 boxes)

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: These sheets were developed by Dwight Large during his parish ministry for each service and were distributed after worship as people went home. They were intended to supplement the Sunday worship service and to extend the 'church experience' throughout the week. Each sheet contains a brief summary of the sermon (50-60 words), Bible verses for each weekday, additional readings related to the sermon theme, and suggested activities to reinforce Christian awareness and growth. An index sermons (1967-1971) follows the "What Then Are We To Do?" sheets. Material donated by Mrs. Frances Large.

did.unittitle: Lay, Corliss and Lillian

bioghist.head: Biographical / Historical
bioghist.p: Corliss Wilkes Lay (1862-) and Lillian Matthews Lay were missionaries serving under the American Board of Commissioners for Foreign Missions, Maratha Mission, in India from 1890 to 1893, stationed primarily in Ahmednagar and Mumbai [Bombay]. After their return to the U.S. in 1893 the Lays worked at Yankton College in South Dakota. Corliss Lay was a student at Yale Divinity School 1888-1889 and graduated from Chicago Theological Seminary in 1890.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: A detailed summary of the collection is available in the first folder. Letters in the collection describe the Lays' work teaching Indian girls and boys and being in charge of a church that had up to 800 students in its congregation. Their candid, often negative, impressions of India may be of interest to researchers in ethnographic studies. Topics in the letters include persistent sickness at the mission school, the status of women in India, run-ins with English soldiers and companies, child marriage, agriculture, missionary politics, and so forth.

Martin, Ebenezer

bioghist.head: Biographical / Historical
bioghist.p: Ebenezer Martin (1732–1795) was born in Windham County, Connecticut. Martin graduated from Yale College in 1756 and went on to pursue a career in ministry. During his studies at Yale, Martin met and married his wife Susanna (Plumb) Martin, and together they had seven children. One of these children, Joseph Plumb Martin who was raised by his maternal grandparents, famously wrote and published a narrative describing his experience as a soldier for the Continental Army in the Revolutionary War. The Reverend Ebenezer Martin's began his ministerial career as the founding preacher of the First Congregational Church in Becket, Massachusetts in 1759, where he remained until his dismissal in 1764. Throughout his life, Rev. Martin struggled to maintain steady employment, and was dismissed from his position as minister on multiple occasions due to his tendency to accumulate debt and fall into disagreements with members of the congregations he served. He moved around frequently, living in Connecticut, Massachusetts, Pennsylvania, and New York throughout his adult life, before he died in 1795.

did.unittitle: Journal

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: This journal, belonging to Ebenezer Martin, contains entries written by Martin on a daily basis from January to December in 1794. Written on pages interleaved in a copy of the 1794 edition of The Balloon Almanac , journal entries include Martin's account of his daily life as a pastor to a small congregation on the Susquehanna River near Towanda, Pennsylvania. He reflects on his day-to-day life from the activities he engaged in to those with whom he interacted, as well as his thoughts and feelings.

bioghist.head: Biographical / Historical
bioghist.p: Matsumoto (1913-1979) was born in Hokkaido, Japan and graduated from Meiji Gakuin University. He went to the U.S. for graduate work at Union Theological Seminary in New York and worked as General Secretary of the Japanese Student Christian Association. Upon his release he was named executive assistant to the secretary of Committee on Resettlement of Japanese-Americans for the Federal Council of Churches and Home Missions Council of North America. Matsumoto received Ed.D. degree from Columbia Univesity in 1949 and returned to live in Japan in 1950, where he was a Professor of English at Meiji Gakuin University.

bioghist.head: Biographical / Historical
bioghist.p: Mattoon was born May 5, 1816 in Champion, New York. In 1842, he graduated from Union College and from Princeton Theological Seminary in 1846. He was ordained as an evangelist on February 11, 1846 by the Presbytery of Troy. Dr. Mattoon was a missionary in Bangkok, Thailand (Siam) for 20 years. As a missionary he was as an interpreter to the King of Siam and organized the first Presbyterian Church of Siam. While in Cambodia, he started The Boys' School in Bangkok and translated the New Testament into Thai (Siamese). From 1870 to 1886, Dr. Stephen Mattoon served as first President of Johnson C. did.unittitle: Monrad, Anna

bioghist.head: Biographical / Historical
bioghist.p: Anna Marie Monrad was born in Karere, New Zealand. She graduated from Rockford College in 1906 and attended university in Denmark for a year in 1914. She began work as a cataloger in the Yale Library system in 1906 and was responsible for classifying the Day Missions Library of Yale Divinity School.

The material within Monrad's collection relates to her relief work in the immediate aftermath of World War II. Working with Yale Divinity students, various churches in New Haven (Dixwell Congregational Church and St. John's Episcopal Church), and the Society of Friends, Monrad facilitated the sending of clothing and food packages to contacts in Europe. She officially served on the New Haven Committee for CARE (Cooperative for American Remittances in Europe), which formed in 1945 to provide surplus American military rations to Europeans. CARE worked through established networks of humanitarian organizations, including the American Friends Service Committee. Anna Monrad, however, worked to efficiently transport aid to her contacts in Europe regardless of the organization—using the Caritas SAFE (Save a Friend in Europe) packages, the Meals for Millions program, and sending personal items to respond to the specific expressed needs of her contacts. In a fundraising letter which Monrad retained, Timothy P. Haworth called the members of the New Haven F.O.R. and the Society of Friends to action, writing, "the pipelines of the UNRRA should be filled to overflowing, the smaller pipelines of private agencies should be stuffed, and those tiny personal pipelines of individual to individual should be filled to the brim."

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: The documentation in this collection relates to Anna Monrad's post-World War II relief work. It mostly dates from 1946-1949 and is written in English, Italian, French, Finnish, and German. Monrad's contacts requested goods, expressed their gratitude, and narrated their own experiences of war and the immediate postwar period. The collected correspondence provides insight into subjective experiences of violence, hunger, internment, migration, and the rapidly changing political landscape of postwar Europe and a divided Germany.

did.unittitle: About the collection

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: A detailed description of the contents of the collection, including names of individuals involved, is contained in the first folder. Letters from a number of individuals involved in the relief efforts are included in the collection.

scopecontent.p: Includes domestic fundraising and organizational correspondence including with Ruth Bainton, receipts of deliveries abroad; a listing of materials typically included in a relief package, and a newspaper clipping related to the New Haven Committee for CARE.

Correspondence of Bainton includes letters from Heinz Horst Schrey and his wife Marianne, Soren and Keena Vestigian, and Gerhard Ritter, among others. See the Roland H. scopecontent.p: Book containing thirteen letters or narrative sketches written by Morris during the period 1820 to 1824. The letters are addressed to "Rev. and dear Sir" or "Dear friend." Letters from Madeira, Cape Town, Sri Lanka (Ceylon), and Chennai (Madras) were written on Morris' voyage to Kolkata (Calcutta) (1820 March-July). Eight letters/sketches describe Morris' work and travels in India. These writings provide valuable accounts of social customs, weather and the natural surroundings in India, as well as the perils of sea travel and the activities of early missionaries.

bioghist.head: Biographical / Historical
bioghist.p: Clark V. Poling (1910-1943) graduated from Yale Divinity School in 1936. He was a minister of the Reformed Church in America serving in Schenectady, NY when World War II began and he volunteered as an Army chaplain. He was one of four chaplains on the transport ship Dorchester , which was hit by a German torpedo on February 2, 1943. The four chaplains were instrumental in organizing the evacuation of soldiers on the ship but several of the lifeboats had been damaged and the chaplains and 672 soldiers went down with the sinking ship. Poling and the other chaplains were posthumously awarded the Distinguished Service Cross and the Purple Heart and received national acclaim for their actions.

did.unittitle: Ralph, Victoria A.

bioghist.head: Biographical / Historical
bioghist.p: Victoria A. Ralph (1870-1967) lived her entire life in New Jersey and worked as a schoolteacher. In 1932 she attended the 11th World Sunday School Convention in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, a convention with thousands of attendees and representatives from fifty countries. Victoria toured around South America with a group of fellow attendees, going to Uruguay, Argentina, and Chile before heading home to the East Coast via Panama and Cuba. She recorded detailed descriptions of location, botany, culture, and history in a travel journal, full of pasted-in images and articles.

Ramseyer, Friedrich August

bioghist.head: Biographical / Historical
bioghist.p: Friedrich August "Fritz" Ramseyer, missionary with the Basel Evangelical Mission Society in Ghana (Gold Coast), was born on October 7, 1840 in Switzerland and died on August 6, 1914. He was a builder was sent to the Gold Coast by the Basel Mission Society in 1864 to assist in putting up more buildings for the Presbyterian Church of Ghana at Akropong. In 1869 he was captured by the Asante, together with his wife Rosa Louise Ramseyer , Basel mission technical staff, Johannes Kühne and French trader, Marie-Joseph Bonnat. Ramseyer was released in 1874 and pioneered the Christian mission in Kumasi and the rest of Asante, also planting churches in Abetifi. Apart from his evangelism, Ramseyer was instrumental in the expansion of opportunities in the fields of education and artisan industry training.

Russell, Letty Mandeville

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: The main collection of Letty Russell papers is part of the Archives of Women in Theological Scholarship collection at The Burke Library at Union Theological Seminary, New York.

bioghist.head: Biographical / Historical
bioghist.p: Letty Mandeville Russell (1929-2007) was a longtime member of the Yale Divinity School faculty and was considered one of the world's foremost feminist theologians. Russell was a leader for many years in the ecumenical movement and had remained active in ecumenical circles until her death, working for the World Council of Churches and the World YWCA. She was one of the first women ordained in the United Presbyterian Church and served the East Harlem Protestant Parish in New York City 1952-1968, including 10 years as pastor of the Presbyterian Church of the Ascension. She served on the YDS faculty 1974-2001. In retirement, she continued to teach some courses at the school.

Scudder, John

bioghist.head: Biographical / Historical
bioghist.p: Scudder was the first medical missionary of the American Board of Commissioners for Foreign Missions (ABCFM), appointed to Sri Lanka (Ceylon) in 1819. Stationed among the Tamils of Jaffna peninsula he had a ministry of evangelism together with a hospital, day and boarding schools, and training of medical students. In 1836 Scudder was transferred to Madras, India. He spent 1842 to 1846 on furlough in the United States, where he promoted missions at churches. Returning to India, he worked three years at Madura, then at Madras until 1845, when he went to South Africa on health leave. He died in South Africa in 1855.

Shelton, Albert L.

bioghist.head: Biographical / Historical
bioghist.p: Albert Leroy Shelton was born in Indiana in 1875 and raised in Kansas. He attended State Normal in Emporia Kansas, where he met his wife Flora, whom he married in 1899. He graduated with a medical degreee from Kentucky University. In 1903, Albert, Flora, and their two daughters Dorris and Dorothy moved to central Asia. Shelton worked as a missionary doctor and preacher with the Foreign Christian Missionary Society of the Disciples of Christ first in Tachienlu before moving to Batang in 1908, located in the Kham region of Tibet where they established a hospital and mission station. The Shelton family's tenure in the Kham region overlapped with a time of violence between Chinese soldiers and Tibetans fighting in resistance. Shelton was kidnapped for ransom in 1920 and held for more than two months. In 1922, he was shot and killed near Batang. The Shelton family wrote extensively on their experiences in Tibet: Albert Shelton wrote Pioneer in Tibet among other titles, Flora wrote Sunshine and Shadow on the Tibetan Border , and Doris wrote the semi-autobiographical novel Sue in Tibet .

bioghist.head: Biographical / Historical
bioghist.p: The Shorrocks were Christian Church (Disciples of Christ) missionaries in Japan. Hal Shorrock graduated from Yale Divinity School in 1952. After teaching English in a Tokyo Christian secondary school beginning in 1947 and organizing and participating in the first Japan National Christian Council-sponsored international Christian work camps in 1949-50, Shorrock went on to direct Church World Service's extensive relief and rehabilitation programs in Japan and then Korea. In 1963 Shorrock was named vice president for financial affairs of International Christian University (ICU) in Tokyo before returning to the United States in 1969 and he also spent four post-retirement years in Japan as ICU's dean of international affairs.

bioghist.p: Born in Scotland, 1841, Stevenson came to the America in 1863 by way of Canada. Following a period in Minnesota he served under the American Missionary Assoociation in Texas, teaching freed slaves, including as principal of Barnes Institute in Galveston. In 1872 he entered Yale Divinity School and received a B.D. in 1875. He served Congregational churches in Ellsworth, Connecticut (1875-1879), Shenandoah, Iowa (1880-1885) and Waterloo, Iowa (1896-1898). Later in life he lost his voice but continued to communicate via writing. He was the editor of the Woman's Standard , a suffragist newspaper, and wrote editorials for the Waterloo Courier . He died in 1912. For more detailed biographical information see a statement by his great granddaughter Flora Beach Burlingame in the first folder of the collection.

Stuntz Allen Family

bioghist.head: Biographical / Historical
bioghist.p: The daughter of Methodist missionaries Clyde Bronson Stuntz and Florence (Sally) Watters Stuntz, Elizabeth (Betty) Stuntz Allen grew up primarily in Lahore, at that time part of India but now Pakistan. Betty graduated from the Woodstock School in Mussoorie, India in 1942 and attended Smith College in Northampton, Massachusetts, graduating in 1947. She received a degree in Social Administration from Western Reserve University in Cleveland in 1949. While preparing at Hartford Seminary to go to India as a missionary herself—marking the third generation of missionaries to India in her family—Betty met Daniel Dorchester Allen, the son of a Methodist pastor. Before accepting his own call to India, Dan graduated in 1946 Yale College and 1949 from Yale Divinity School. After moving to India, Dan and Betty married in the presence of her parents in Lahore in 1950. From 1949 to 1969 they worked for the Methodist Board of Foreign Missions in various capacities throughout India in development and educational work: in Delhi, Punjab, and Woodstock. After eleven moves in twenty years and the births of their four children, Dan and Betty settled in Connecticut where Dan continued to minister in local congregations in New England and Betty with United Methodist Women for the next twenty years.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: The Stuntz-Allen Family Papers contain materials from multiple generations, underscoring the abundance of missionaries within the extended Stuntz family. The gathered correspondence contains a letter from Betty's grandfather, Homer C. Stuntz, as well as substantial correspondence from Clyde Bronson and Florence Watters Stuntz addressed to Betty during her time at Smith College. In the letters, dating from 1945 until 1949, the Stuntzes describe their experiences and advocacy during the Partition of India (1947-1948). On her mother's side, materials from Betty's 1989 trip to China to celebrate the centennial of Ijishan (Wuhu General) Hospital, relate to her late aunt, medical missionary Hyla S. Watters (RG 327). Further materials, such as the reunion binder from the Woodstock School class of 1942, provide insight into the varied lives of missionary children in the latter half of the twentieth century.

did.unittitle: Summers, William

bioghist.head: Biographical / Historical
bioghist.p: Methodist missionary (1855-1888). One of a group of missionaries sent by Bishop William Taylor to Angola in 1885 to begin building a chain of missions across Africa. Summers set out from the mission station at Malange (now Malanje) in 1886 and made his way to Luluabourg (present-day Kananga, Democratic Republic of Congo). Summers spent his last days attempting to found a mission school among the Bashilange people of the southeastern Congo.

did.unittitle: Handwritten journal with typed transcript and summary by bookdealer. Almost daily entries describe Summers' journey from Luluabourg heading for village of the Bashilange chief Kasongo beginning in 1887; meetings with Africa leaders; military actions; etc. until his death in 1888.

The issue of an appeal was caught up in the question of how many people could be accommodated and also how to avoid having North Atlantic people over-represented at the vent. This file also includes many of the meeting notes on representation size and distribution, as Taylor was drawn deeply into that process by staffing a working group on it. Todd, William

bioghist.head: Biographical / Historical
bioghist.p: William Todd was born in Marcellus, NY on March 8, 1801. He graduated from Hamilton College in 1821 and from Auburn Seminary in 1824. After serving as pastor for three years in Benton, NY and three years in West Dresden, NY, he was appointed a missionary of the American Board of Commissioners for Foreign Missions. He embarked with Messrs. Apthorp, Hoisington, Hutchings, and Dr. Ward, at Boston, July 1, 1833, arriving in Madras [now Chennai], India on October 12, 1833. He served under the ABCFM Ceylon Mission from October 28, 1833 at Panditeripo [now Pandatharippu, Sri Lanka] until July 21, 1834 when he moved to Madura [now Madurai], India to form the ABCFM Madura Mission with Henry Hoisington. From January 1839 he was stationed in Shevagunga, near Madura. He left the mission because of poor health, arriving back in the U.S. in June 1839. He died in Kansas on August 10, 1874.

did.unittitle: Nine letters, some including journal entries, written by Todd to his brothers and parents in the U.S.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: These letters and journal entries provide subtantive detail about about Todd's sea journey to India in 1833, his work with the ABCFM Ceylon Mission including at Pandateripo, his founding of the Madura Mission in 1834, and work in Shevagunga [now Sivaganga, Tamil Nadu, India].

Walls, Andrew F.

bioghist.head: Biographical / Historical
bioghist.p: Andrew Finlay Walls was born in 1928 in New Milton, England. Following his education at the University of Oxford, Walls taught at Fourah Bay College in Sierra Leone from 1957 to 1962 and the University of Nigeria, Nsukka from 1962 to 1965. He taught at the University of Aberdeen from 1966 to 1986 when he moved to the University of Edinburgh. Walls was the founder and director of the Centre for the Study of Christianity in the Non-Western World (now known as the Centre for the Study of World Christianity), first at the University of Aberdeen in 1982, before moving it to the University of Edinburgh in 1987. He co-founded the Yale-Edinburgh Group on World Christianity and the History of Mission with Lamin Sanneh in 1992.

bioghist.head: Biographical / Historical
bioghist.p: Warren graduated from the University of Sydney in 1954 and started her overseas missionary service in 1957 in Busan (Pusan), Korea. In 1959 she began work with the Leprosy Mission International in Hong Kong, learning techniques of reconstructive surgery. After ten years she made her base in central Thailand and traveled widely to run training programs in hospitals. She became an international authority in the care of neuropathic limbs, especially due to leprosy and diabetes, and in recontructive surgery.

bioghist.head: Biographical / Historical
bioghist.p: Helen Maria Wells was raised in Oneida County, New York, and married David White in October 1836. In December 1836, Helen and David departed for what was then called the "colony of Maryland" at Cape Palmas, Liberia to work as missionaries with the ABCFM. According to the 1836 Maryland Colonization Journal, "Mr. White took with him a printing press, and a highly respectable coloured man as a printer, fully competent to take charge of it." Shortly after their arrival in West Africa, Rev. David White and Helen White died from fever in January 1837.

Williams, Leighton

bioghist.head: Biographical / Historical
bioghist.p: Leighton Williams was the pastor of Amity Baptist Church in New York City from 1887-1917. In 1892 he was the co-founder with Walter Rauschenbusch of The Brotherhood of the Kingdom, a non-denominational group of authors, clergy and other leading thinkers from a variety of Christian Protestant backgrounds who were advocates of the Social Gospel. Meetings of the Brotherhood were held at Williams' home in Marlborough, New York annually until 1915. Group members presented papers, talks, and debates related to the Social Gospel.

Wyland, Benjamin Franklin

bioghist.head: Biographical / Historical
bioghist.p: Benjamin F. Wyland, son of Frank and Molly Griffith Wyland, was born on March 16, 1882, in Harlan, Shelby County, Iowa. He received his Ph.D. from the University of Iowa in 1905 and his B.D. from Yale in 1908. Wyland married Ada Beach on January 14, 1909, in New Haven, Connecticut. They had four children together. After being ordained as a minister in the Congregational Church in 1908, Rev. Wyland served as associate pastor at the Tompkins Avenue Church, 1910-1917. During 1917-1918 he was religious editor of the New York Tribune . In 1918, Wyland served in the pulpit of Union Church in Worcester, Massachusetts. In 1923 he was an exchange preacher between the U.S. and England. He held this position again in 1933. From 1926 to 1936, Rev. Wyland was pastor at the First Plymouth Congregational Church of Lincoln, Nebraska. During his tenure, a new church building was completed. After leaving Lincoln in 1936, Wyland served three years as a pastor in Brooklyn, New York. During World War II he became liaison Chaplain for the Council of Churches of Maryland. After the war, Wyland moved to St. Petersburg, Florida, where he continued to serve his church and where he was also deeply involved in numerous civil rights and social welfare projects. Ada Wyland died in 1953 and Benjamin then married Mildred (Carmichael) Oeschger. Mildred died in 1978. Rev. Benjamin F. Wyland died in St. Petersburg, Florida, on July 24, 1986. He is buried in the Harlan Cemetery at Harlan, Iowa, along with his second wife, Mildred.
Source: Nebraska State Historical Society

Younger, George Dana

bioghist.head: Biographical / Historical
bioghist.p: George Dana Younger (1926-2001) graduated from Yale Divinity School in 1950. He was a minister, theologian, and educator. His papers are held in the American Baptist Historical Society archives at Mercer University.

did.unittitle: Set of "round robin" letters from Younger and fellow students at Yale Divinity School describing their biographical past, and their work and spiritual / professional development, plus personal letters to Younger from members of the group.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: A group of thirteen Yale Divinity School students apparently agreed to share their "personal histories" with each other. Individuals represented in this collection are Dale Beittel, Fitz Dodson, John C. Heinrich, George Lindbeck, James Martin, Niels C. Nielsen, John Riebel, William Sengel, and George Younger.

did.unittitle: Zanisi, Angelo Saverio

bioghist.head: Biographical / Historical
bioghist.p: Zanisi worked as a missionary in North Malabar, India from 1951-1956. He moved to the Philippines in 1956, working at the Papal Embassy in Manila for a year and then beginning a new Mission on the island of Samar in the town of Jipapad. He left the Philippines in 1983.

Zorn, Herbert M.

bioghist.head: Biographical / Historical
bioghist.p: Zorn served with the Theological Education Fund (TEF) based in London from 1972 to 1975. He was coordinator of a study on the viability of theological education in the majority world, which was published as "Viability in Context"

did.unittitle: Photograph album from Japan

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: The photographs depict the lives of American Episcopal missionaries both at home in the United States (Illinois, Iowa, Michigan) and in many locations throughout Japan. Further images depict both American and Japanese mission workers in school settings, conferences, and traveling. The families depicted include the Dobbins, Watson, Draper, Smith, Nicodemus, and Rotzel families among others.
